_meta.descricao: Marriage, consecrated life, ordained ministry, and lay life as concrete forms of the universal call to holiness.
_meta.aviso: An introductory overview; the Religious Orders category deals with specific congregations, and Sacraments deals with marriage and holy orders as sacramental rites.
fontes_gerais: Second Vatican Council, Lumen Gentium, chap. IV-VI

itens.resumo: Every Christian receives from God a personal and specific call to live and to love in a particular way, within the one common call to holiness.
itens.corpo: "Vocation" (from the Latin vocare, "to call") designates the personal and specific call that God addresses to each person for a concrete form of life and love, within the universal and common call to holiness that applies to every baptized person, without exception. The Church recognizes different states of life through which this call is made concrete — marriage, consecrated life, ordained ministry, and lay life in the world —, none of them superior in human dignity to the others, although distinct in their specific form and mission. Discerning one's own vocation is a central task of the spiritual life, generally matured through prayer, spiritual direction, and concrete life experience.

itens.resumo: The covenant of love between a man and a woman, raised by Christ to the dignity of a sacrament, is the path to holiness for the vast majority of the baptized and a full vocation — not a lesser stage compared to consecrated life.
itens.corpo:
Christian marriage is not merely a social or civil contract, but a true vocation and sacrament: the covenant of exclusive and definitive love between a man and a woman, open to life, by which the spouses sanctify one another and educate their children in the faith. The Code of Canon Law defines it as the covenant "by which a man and a woman establish between themselves a partnership of the whole of life, which is ordered by its nature to the good of the spouses and the procreation and education of offspring," raised by Christ the Lord to the dignity of a sacrament between the baptized (can. 1055).

The great doctrinal turning point came with the Second Vatican Council. The pastoral constitution Gaudium et Spes devotes an entire chapter to the dignity of marriage and the family (nos. 47–52) and presents marriage as an "intimate partnership of married life and love," in which true love between the spouses involves mutual self-giving and integrates the sexual and affective dimensions according to the divine plan. Before the Council, the 1917 Code ranked the "ends" of marriage: the procreation and education of offspring as the primary end, and the good of the spouses and mutual help as the secondary end. Gaudium et Spes, by describing marriage above all as a communion of life and love, introduced the expression bonum coniugum — the good of the spouses — and shifted the axis from a hierarchy of ends to mutual self-giving and sanctification. The 1983 Code reflected this change, placing "the good of the spouses" and "the procreation and education of offspring" side by side in the canonical definition itself (can. 1055, §1), with no distinction of primacy between them. The controversy over whether the bonum coniugum and the bonum prolis are "ends" or "properties" of marriage has run through later canonical theology, discussed in numerous studies on the 1917 and 1983 codes.

It was Saint Thomas Aquinas, cited in Familiaris Consortio, who brought the educational mission of parents close to the priestly ministry: some propagate and preserve the spiritual life "by a solely spiritual ministry: this is the task of the sacrament of Orders; others do so with regard to both bodily and spiritual life" through the sacrament of marriage, "which unites man and woman so that they may have offspring and bring them up to the worship of God." The apostolic exhortation Familiaris Consortio (1981), by John Paul II, developed this theology: the duty of education receives from the sacrament of marriage the dignity of a true "ministry" of the Church at the service of building up its members, and the family is called the "domestic church" (cf. Lumen Gentium 11).

Being the state of life of the vast majority of the baptized, marriage is an ordinary and full path to holiness, not a "lesser" stage compared to consecrated life. The Council explicitly insisted that all states of life are a vocation to live Christian charity and holiness fully. It is worth recalling that Catholic doctrine has always joined the sacramental character of marriage with the particular value of consecrated virginity: Saint John Chrysostom, cited in Familiaris Consortio, compared virginity to a special flower, without this diminishing the dignity of marriage, and the Council of Trent itself, in Session XXIV, firmly reaffirmed the sacramentality and indissolubility of the bond against the errors of the time.

itens.resumo: A stable form of life by which the faithful, under the action of the Holy Spirit, publicly profess the evangelical counsels of chastity, poverty and obedience and consecrate themselves totally to God — an eschatological sign of the Kingdom.
itens.corpo:
Consecrated life is defined by the 1983 Code of Canon Law (can. 573, §1) as "a stable form of living by which the faithful, following Christ more closely under the action of the Holy Spirit, are totally dedicated to God who is loved most of all, so that, having been dedicated by a new and special title to his honor, to the building up of the Church, and to the salvation of the world, they strive for the perfection of charity in the service of the Kingdom of God and, having been made an outstanding sign in the Church, foretell the heavenly glory." It is not, therefore, a simple choice of individual piety, but a state of life recognized and regulated by the Church, which can. 574 describes as belonging "to the life and holiness of the Church" and as something that "is to be fostered and promoted by all in the Church."

The doctrinal foundation lies in the Second Vatican Council. The dogmatic constitution Lumen Gentium devotes chapter VI to religious: the evangelical counsels of "chastity consecrated to God, poverty and obedience" are presented as "a divine gift which the Church received from her Lord" and which has given rise, "as on a tree growing from a seed planted by God and wondrously branching out in the field of the Lord, to various forms of solitary or community life" (LG 43). Number 44 spells out the logic of consecration: by Baptism the Christian has already died to sin and been consecrated to God; by the profession of the counsels, however, he is "freed from the impediments which might draw him away from the fervor of charity" and is consecrated "more intimately to divine service", so that "this consecration will be the more perfect, the more the firmness and stability of the bonds" sustain it. The decree Perfectae Caritatis completed this basis, guiding the renewal of religious life with regard to fidelity to the original charism and adaptation to the conditions of the times.

The Latin theological tradition arranges the three counsels as "poverty, chastity and obedience", a radicalization of the baptismal self-gift that configures the consecrated person to Christ who is poor, chaste and obedient and visibly anticipates, already in this life, the eschatological reality of the Kingdom, where "they neither marry nor are given in marriage" (Mt 22:30). Historically, before the Council, the order in which the vows were professed was obedience, chastity and poverty — obedience being considered the most demanding, as a renunciation of one's own freedom, and poverty being seen above all in its external dimension. Later theology began from the undivided heart (LG 42), emphasizing that the total gift of one's being precedes the distinction of the three counsels.

It is important to distinguish consecrated life from religious life in the strict sense. The umbrella term includes religious institutes (can. 607–709), marked by public profession of vows, common life and a certain degree of separation from the world; secular institutes, whose members live in the world and work for its sanctification "from within"; and also the individual forms recognized by law: the hermit, who publicly professes the counsels into the hands of the diocesan bishop (can. 603), and the order of virgins (can. 604). Vows may be solemn, typical of the older and more austere orders, or simple, characteristic of congregations, which in general allow the member to retain ownership, though not the use, of personal goods.

Far from being a flight from the world, consecrated life is a prophetic witness that God is enough and that the goods of this life — wealth, absolute autonomy, married life — are not the ultimate end of human existence. It remains, however, a gift that knows numerical variations: according to the Pontifical Yearbook 2025 and the Annuarium Statisticum Ecclesiae 2023, the number of professed women religious in the world fell from 599,228 (2022) to 589,423 (2023), a decrease attributed above all to the high proportion of elderly sisters, while the number of departures from religious life proved less significant in the period.

itens.titulo: The Ordained Ministry as a Vocation
itens.resumo: Bishops, priests, and deacons receive, through the sacrament of Holy Orders, a special configuration to Christ, Head and Servant of the Church.
itens.corpo: The sacrament of Holy Orders confers on bishops, priests, and deacons a special sacramental configuration to Christ, enabling them to act "in persona Christi Capitis" — in the person of Christ, Head of the Church — above all in the celebration of the sacraments and in the authoritative proclamation of the Word. Unlike marriage and consecrated life, which primarily concern the personal sanctification of those who live them, Holy Orders is essentially oriented toward the service of the ecclesial community: the ordained receives the gift not for himself, but to build up the Body of Christ through teaching, worship, and pastoral governance.

itens.resumo: The specific vocation of the lay faithful is to sanctify temporal realities — family, work, politics, culture — from within.
itens.corpo: The Second Vatican Council, in the constitution Lumen Gentium, clearly defined the proper vocation of the lay faithful: to seek the Kingdom of God "by engaging in temporal affairs and by directing them according to God's will," living the faith precisely in the midst of the ordinary realities of the world — profession, family, civic life, culture — not in spite of them, but through them. The lay person is neither a "second-class religious" nor a mere subordinate collaborator of the clergy, but has a proper and irreplaceable mission to imbue the temporal structures of society with the spirit of the Gospel, from within and with competence proper to their field of activity.

itens.resumo: A little-known form of consecration: people who profess the evangelical counsels while remaining fully immersed in ordinary secular life.
itens.corpo: Formally recognized by Pius XII in 1947, secular institutes gather men and women who profess the evangelical counsels of poverty, chastity, and obedience, as religious do, but without community life or a distinctive habit, remaining engaged in their ordinary professions and secular environments, often without their colleagues or neighbors knowing of their consecration. They thus combine the radicalism of the vows with a discreet, lay presence at the heart of secular structures, and are considered an original bridge between traditional consecrated life and the lay vocation in the world.

itens.resumo: The Order of Virgins and the consecration of widows, attested since apostolic times, were restored by the post-conciliar liturgical reform for women who consecrate themselves to God outside community religious life.
itens.corpo:
The Order of Virgins (Ordo virginum) and the consecration of widows (Ordo viduarum) are very ancient forms of consecrated life, attested already in the first centuries of Christianity. The Instruction Ecclesiae Sponsae Imago, published on July 4, 2018 by the Congregation for Institutes of Consecrated Life and Societies of Apostolic Life and signed by Cardinal João Braz de Aviz and Archbishop José Rodríguez Carballo, places the origin of the Order of Virgins in apostolic times: since then, the image of the Church as the bride of Christ (cf. Eph 5:23-32; Rev 19:7-9) has been manifested in a singular way in the lives of those women who, with spousal love, dedicate themselves to the Lord in virginity. The patristic tradition bears witness to this flourishing: Saint Cyprian of Carthage, in his work on virginity, calls virgins the "flower of the Church's seed, the grace and ornament of spiritual endowment" and affirms that the more the number of virgins grows, the more the joy of mother Church grows; Saint Ambrose, in *De Virginibus*, dedicated to his sister Marcellina, presents the Virgin Mary as the model and "image of virginity" for all consecrated women.

Throughout history, both the Order of Virgins and the rite of consecration of widows fell into disuse. The Order of Virgins was restored on the initiative of Saint Paul VI: on May 31, 1970, the Sacred Congregation for Divine Worship, by his mandate, promulgated the new Rite of Consecration to a Life of Virginity (Ordo consecrationis virginum). The decree presented consecrated women as the "image of the Church, bride of Christ." Before that, virginal consecration was, in practice, reserved to nuns; the new rite opened the possibility of receiving it also to women who remain in their ordinary context of life, and not in a religious community.

Juridically, the Order of Virgins has its own canon, canon 604 of the 1983 Code of Canon Law, according to which virgins, "expressing the holy resolution of following Christ more closely, are consecrated to God by the diocesan Bishop according to the approved liturgical rite, are betrothed mystically to Christ, the Son of God, and are dedicated to the service of the Church," and they may associate together in order to observe their resolution more faithfully. The Ordo virginum has no founder other than the Church herself, and its only superior, in each diocese, is the diocesan Bishop, with no intermediate authority. Consecrated virgins are neither consecrated lay persons nor religious: they are among the forms of consecrated life, fully inserted in the particular Church. As for widows, the 1983 Code dedicates no specific canon to them, a notable gap, since the Ordo viduarum has apostolic roots (cf. 1 Tim 5:5, 9-10; 1 Cor 7:8) and a discipline of its own over several centuries; the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (1990, can. 570) refers to the particular law of each *sui iuris* Church the establishment of consecrated virgins or widows who profess chastity in the world. While the Order of Virgins has had, since 1970, a Ritual approved by the Holy See, the Order of Widows still has no Ritual valid for the whole Church, but only particular rites approved by the bishops of the dioceses where they exist.

In Brazil, according to the Committee of Consecrated Virgins of the CNBB, as of December 2023 there were estimated to be 206 living consecrated virgins, with 323 consecrations carried out since the renewal of the rite. Worldwide, an approximate statistic from 2016, during the Year of Consecrated Life, indicated more than five thousand consecrated virgins, in continuous growth, present on every continent. The Instruction Ecclesiae Sponsae Imago underlines the traits of this vocation: absolute gratuitousness, the Marian profile (Mary being the Virgo virginum), and openness to the gift of spiritual motherhood, lived out in service to the particular Church, in prayer, in penance, and in works of charity, with the consecrated women providing for their own support through the fruit of their work. In 2020, the 50th anniversary of the Rite would prompt an international gathering of consecrated virgins in Rome.

itens.resumo: Restored by the Second Vatican Council as a stable degree of the ordained ministry, also open to married men.
itens.corpo: For centuries, the diaconate in the West had become almost exclusively a transitional stage on the way to the presbyterate. The Second Vatican Council authorized its restoration as a permanent and stable degree of the sacrament of Holy Orders, open to both celibate and married men (provided they were already married before ordination, and may not marry again after ordination should they become widowers). Permanent deacons exercise ministries of charity, of liturgical service (they may baptize, preside at weddings and funerals, and preach), and of the proclamation of the Word, generally combining the ministry with a secular profession and family life.

itens.resumo: The spiritual process by which a person seeks to identify, with freedom and prayer, to which state of life God is calling him or her.
itens.corpo: Vocational discernment is the personal and spiritual process, usually accompanied by assiduous prayer, qualified spiritual direction, and concrete life experience, by which a person seeks to identify more clearly to which specific state of life God is calling him or her. It is not simply a matter of choosing among indifferent options, but of actively seeking, in freedom and interior listening, God's specific will for that person — a process that can take considerable time and frequently involves doubt, interior resistance, and gradual maturing before a definitive and free response.

itens.resumo: A discipline of the Latin Church by which candidates for the presbyterate renounce marriage, uniting themselves to Christ with an undivided heart in order to devote themselves more freely to the service of God and of men.
itens.corpo: Priestly celibacy—the renunciation of marriage by those who prepare for the presbyterate in the Latin Church—is not a dogma of faith nor a requirement of the very nature of the priesthood, but an ecclesiastical discipline with a long tradition, solemnly reaffirmed by the Council of Trent and now codified in canon 277 of the Code of Canon Law. The Second Vatican Council, in the decree Presbyterorum Ordinis, teaches that this celibacy "for the sake of the kingdom of heaven" is a sign and stimulus of pastoral charity, enabling the priest to be united to Christ with an undivided heart and to devote himself more freely and completely to the service of God and of men. The discipline does not apply, it should be noted, to the Eastern Catholic Churches, which maintain the tradition of ordaining married men to the presbyterate as well.

itens.resumo: Poverty, chastity, and obedience, proposed by Christ in the Gospel to those who wish to follow him more closely, are the common foundation on which every form of consecrated life is built.
itens.corpo: Distinct from the commandments, which bind every Christian, the evangelical counsels — perfect chastity for the sake of the Kingdom of Heaven, voluntary poverty, and obedience — are proposed by Christ in the Gospel not as a universal obligation, but as a path of perfection freely offered to those who feel called to follow him more closely. The Catechism of the Catholic Church teaches that it is precisely the public and stable profession of these three counsels, undertaken in an institute recognized by the Church, that technically characterizes "consecrated life" and distinguishes it from other forms of Christian life. Each of the three counsels responds to a fundamental human temptation — attachment to possessions, to pleasure, and to one's own will — and visibly anticipates the definitive freedom of the children of God.

itens.resumo: Recognized by canon 603 of the Code of Canon Law, it allows the faithful to consecrate themselves to God by living in solitude, silence, and penance, under the guidance of the diocesan bishop.
itens.corpo: Alongside communal religious life, the Church formally recognizes the eremitic or anchoritic life as a proper and distinct form of consecrated life: the hermit withdraws more strictly from the world, in the silence of solitude, in assiduous prayer and in penance, devoting his or her life to the praise of God and the salvation of the world. Canon 603 of the Code of Canon Law requires, for this juridical recognition, the public profession of the three evangelical counsels into the hands of the diocesan bishop, confirmed by vow or other sacred bond, and a life lived under the direction of that same bishop — unlike the cenobitic monk, the diocesan hermit does not belong to a religious institute and must, as a rule, provide for his or her own support.

itens.resumo: A canonical category distinct from consecrated life: its members live in common fraternal life and pursue an apostolic purpose proper to the society, without necessarily professing religious vows.
itens.corpo: The Code of Canon Law (canons 731-746) recognizes, alongside religious institutes and secular institutes, a third category: societies of apostolic life, whose members pursue the apostolic purpose proper to the society and, leading a fraternal life in common according to their own manner of living, strive for the perfection of charity through the observance of the constitutions. The fundamental difference from institutes of consecrated life is that the members of a society of apostolic life, at least as a rule, do not take the public religious vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, although some societies provide in their own constitutions for some equivalent sacred bond. Historical examples are the Congregation of the Mission (Vincentians) and the Daughters of Charity.

itens.resumo: Associations of lay people and diocesan clergy who live, in their own state of life in the world, the spirituality and the rule of a religious family, such as the Franciscan or the Carmelite.
itens.corpo: Alongside the "first order" (the religious) and the "second order" (the contemplative women's branches), several medieval religious families gave rise to a "third order" or "secular order": associations of lay faithful — and also diocesan clergy — who, without leaving their ordinary state of life in the world (married, single, widowed), profess to live the spirituality and follow the rule proper to that religious family, adapted to secular life. The best-known example is the Secular Franciscan Order (OFS), founded by Saint Francis of Assisi himself for lay people who could not or did not wish to "abandon the world", but desired to become holy within it by following the Franciscan spirit; other religious families, such as the Carmelite and the Dominican, have analogous secular branches.

itens.resumo: A religious consecrated by the vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience who does not receive the sacrament of Holy Orders, living out his vocation through work, communal prayer, and fraternal witness.
itens.corpo: Not every religious is a priest: the "brother" is the professed religious — of temporary or perpetual vows — who is ordained neither priest nor deacon, living his consecration wholly through fraternal witness, work, and prayer in community, without exercising the sacramental ministry proper to the ordained. In the early centuries of monastic life, most monks were, in this sense, laymen — the priestly ordination of a good part of religious is a later historical development — and institutes such as the Marist Brothers or the Brothers of the Christian Schools were founded precisely to be composed, entirely, of non-ordained brothers. The Church insists that this specific vocation is not a "lesser" or incomplete stage on the way to the priesthood, but a full and complete form, in itself, of consecrated life.

itens.resumo: The formal path of initiation into a religious institute, from the period of the novitiate to temporary vows and, finally, to perpetual profession.
itens.corpo: Before assuming the evangelical counsels in a stable manner, those who enter a religious institute go through the novitiate — a period which, according to canon 646 of the Code of Canon Law, is intended to enable the novice to better know his or her vocation and the proper vocation of the institute, to have a concrete experience of its way of life, and to prove his or her intention and suitability, lasting a minimum of one year and a maximum of two. Once the novitiate is completed, the religious makes temporary profession — for a determined period, generally between three and six years —, which is renewable, until, after his or her vocational maturity has been assessed, he or she is admitted to perpetual profession, a definitive and stable bond by which he or she is fully and irrevocably incorporated into the chosen institute.

itens.titulo: The Common Priesthood of the Faithful
itens.resumo: Every baptized person shares, in his or her own way, in the one priesthood of Christ — a participation that differs in essence, and not merely in degree, from the ministerial priesthood of the ordained.
itens.corpo: The conciliar constitution Lumen Gentium teaches, in number 10, that Christ made the whole baptized people "a kingdom of priests" for God, so that each of the faithful, through the exercise of faith, hope, and charity and through sacramental life, truly shares in the one priesthood of Christ — called the common or baptismal priesthood. The same text affirms, however, that this common priesthood and the ministerial priesthood of the ordained, although both derive from the one priesthood of Christ and are ordered one to another, differ from one another not only in degree but in essence: the ministerial priesthood exists precisely to serve and to develop the common priesthood of the whole People of God, and it neither replaces it nor absorbs it.

itens.titulo: Contemplative Life and Active Life in Consecrated Life
itens.resumo: Within consecrated life, institutes are distinguished by giving priority either to prayer and enclosure or to direct apostolic action among the people of God — two legitimate and complementary ways of living the same calling.
itens.corpo: Not all consecrated life has the same concrete form: institutes of contemplative life — such as the Carthusians, the Trappists, or the Discalced Carmelites — are organized around enclosure, silence, and liturgical and personal prayer as their central and almost exclusive occupation, placing prayer more explicitly at the center of existence. Institutes of active apostolic life — such as the Salesians, the Redemptorists, or many congregations of sisters devoted to education and health care — join communal prayer to a direct and visible apostolic mission among the people, such as teaching, caring for the sick, or evangelization. The apostolic exhortation Vita Consecrata, by Saint John Paul II, teaches that this diversity of forms does not indicate a hierarchy of value between contemplation and action, but the richness of charisms with which the Holy Spirit continues to enrich the Church.

itens.resumo: A required stage on the path to the priesthood, in which the candidate receives the first degree of the sacrament of Holy Orders before being ordained a priest.
itens.corpo: Unlike the permanent diaconate, which is taken up as a stable and definitive vocation, the transitional diaconate is the diaconal ordination received by every candidate for the priesthood as a necessary stage of his own sacramental journey: no one is ordained a priest without first having been ordained a deacon. After completing the studies of philosophy and theology, the future priest exercises the diaconal ministry — preaching, baptizing, assisting at marriages, and liturgical and charitable service — for a relatively brief period, generally between six months and a year, determined by the diocesan bishop or the competent religious superior, before receiving priestly ordination proper.

itens.titulo: The Major Seminary and Priestly Formation
itens.resumo: The house and formative process by which the Church accompanies the discernment and preparation, over several successive stages, of candidates for the ministerial priesthood.
itens.corpo: The major seminary is the institution where the Church welcomes and forms, over several years, candidates for the presbyterate, uniting human, spiritual, intellectual, and pastoral formation. According to the Ratio Fundamentalis Institutionis Sacerdotalis, a document of the Congregation for the Clergy that currently governs this formation throughout the Latin Church, the journey is structured in four successive stages: the propaedeutic stage, devoted to initial vocational discernment and to human and spiritual maturation; the discipleship stage, corresponding to philosophical studies; the configuration stage, corresponding to theology; and the stage of vocational synthesis, of a more directly pastoral character, which precedes ordination. The complete process usually extends over seven to eight years.
